picks.headline: Publishers file lawsuit against Google for AI training
picks.excerpt: Major publishers including Hachette, Cengage and Elsevier sued Google, alleging it used digital copies from Google Books, Google Play and Google Scholar to train its Gemini model without permission. The complaint claims Google internally flagged the practice as 'highly problematic' and warned of billions in potential fines yet proceeded anyway. A rights/consent story shaping whether and how book text feeds AI models.
picks.rationale: A live class action over Gemini training sets a concrete copyright/consent precedent that directly shapes how publishers and authors handle AI-training rights; the suit never had its own card, so it is a genuinely distinct net-new story rather than a rehash of the Bloomsbury earnings round-up's passing mention.

picks.headline: Library News Round-Up, July 2026 (incl. ElevenLabs' AI-narrated Odyssey)
picks.excerpt: Book Riot's July library round-up highlights ElevenLabs releasing an officially licensed AI-narrated edition of The Odyssey using a synthetic Michael Caine voice, alongside broader reading-crisis coverage. The item captures the arrival of licensed synthetic-voice narration in the commercial audiobook market and the job-displacement questions it raises for human narrators. A creative-AI capability landing in mainstream publishing.
picks.rationale: Licensed synthetic-voice narration (Michael Caine) reaching a commercial audiobook release is a net-new creative-AI capability with clear implications for narrators and audio publishers; no Odyssey/ElevenLabs card exists anywhere in the books history, so it is genuinely fresh.
